//: Whether a package has any life at all on modern .NET, which is a different question from what replaces it.
//1: Measured, not guessed: three real ports moved every one of these six web packages regardless of how much a successor covered, from 8 per cent to 68, and kept every library that still ships a modern build.
//2: A package absent from this file is unknown. Unknown is not the same as fine, and nothing is claimed about it.

Microsoft.AspNet.Mvc.why: System.Web.Mvc is built on System.Web, which ASP.NET Core does not have and never will. Staying is not one of the options.

Microsoft.AspNet.Razor.why: The old Razor engine lives in System.Web.Razor and goes with System.Web.

Microsoft.AspNet.WebPages.why: System.Web.WebPages and its helpers are part of the old hosting stack.

Microsoft.Web.Infrastructure.why: It exists to register modules with the old pipeline. Nothing replaces it because nothing needs to.

Microsoft.AspNet.WebApi.Core.why: System.Web.Http is the old Web API stack. ASP.NET Core folds Web API and MVC into one framework.

Microsoft.AspNet.WebApi.WebHost.why: It hosts the old Web API inside IIS through System.Web.

Owin.why: Katana is the .NET Framework host. ASP.NET Core has its own pipeline and does not run it.

Newtonsoft.Json.why: Ships for netstandard2.0 and runs unchanged on modern .NET. Moving to System.Text.Json is a choice somebody makes, not one the runtime makes for them.

log4net.why: Ships for netstandard2.0. Moving to Microsoft.Extensions.Logging is a choice.

Autofac.why: Has supported modern .NET for years and integrates with the built-in container rather than being replaced by it.

EntityFramework.why: EF6 runs on modern .NET since 6.3. Moving to EF Core is a choice, and an expensive one: the query semantics differ in ways that compile and behave differently.

NHibernate.why: Ships for netstandard2.0 and runs on modern .NET.
